attempts.reasoning: TokenBucket._refill added Math.floor(elapsed/1000)*refillPerSec and then reset the timestamp, so partial seconds were discarded and callers polling every 500ms never got tokens at 2/s. The fix accrues tokens continuously as (elapsed/1000)*refillPerSec, caps the total at capacity, and advances `last` only when time actually moved forward. If the clock goes backwards or stands still, no tokens are added and `last` is kept, so the next forward step accrues only from the real last accrual point and nothing is double-counted. tryRemove checks before subtracting, so a rejected request consumes nothing and tokens never go negative. It also rejects negative or NaN costs, which would otherwise mint tokens above capacity. In RateLimiter.retryAfterMs I made the ceiling tolerant of floating-point noise (so an exact 500ms wait isn't reported as 501ms), made sure a non-zero wait is never reported as 0, and handled refillPerSec = 0 explicitly. Each key already has its own bucket and timestamp, so keys stay independent.

attempts.reasoning: TokenBucket._refill credited only whole elapsed seconds (Math.floor(elapsed / 1000)) and then moved the timestamp forward, so partial time was discarded and a client polling every 500ms at refillPerSec=2 never got a token. The fix credits (elapsed / 1000) * refillPerSec continuously and advances `last` by the full elapsed time, so fractional progress carries over between calls. Tokens are capped at capacity after every refill. If the clock goes backwards or stalls, no time is credited and `last` is left at the high-water mark, so time is never counted twice. tryRemove now checks affordability before subtracting, so a rejected call consumes nothing, and the result is clamped at zero. A small epsilon absorbs floating-point drift, such as 0.9999999999 tokens when a full token is due. In RateLimiter, retryAfterMs uses the same epsilon so it returns 0 when a token is effectively available and rounds up correctly otherwise. It also returns Infinity when refillPerSec is 0, which avoids a division by zero. Each key still has its own bucket, so keys remain independent. I did not run the test suite; I checked the visible test by hand: 5 removals drain the bucket, then 500ms at 2/s gives exactly 1 token, so the next tryRemove succeeds.
